extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and prosecuting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including appropriate rationales, how to treat prior art, applicant replies and rebuttal evidence, and analogous-art analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reasons for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness (KSR quoting In re Kahn). The analysis supporting a rejection should be made explicit. See MPEP § 2143 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One permissible rationale supporting obviousness is that known elements can be combined by known methods and would produce predictable outcomes. See MPEP § 2143 for examples and illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness may be supported where a claimed element is merely a predictable substitution of a known element. Evaluate predictability and motivation to substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Using known techniques to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a known technique would be applied to improve similar devices in the same manner, this can support obviousness. Consider whether the technique would have been applied with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a device is ready for improvement and a known technique would predictably improve it, that supports an obviousness conclusion. Document why the device was 'ready for improvement' and predictability of result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: ‘Obvious to try’ with finite predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: (E) “Obvious to try” – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obvious-to-try rationales require a finite, identifiable set of predictable options and a reasonable expectation of success. Avoid applying 'obvious to try' where solutions are numerous/unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different field
rubrics_metrics.description: (F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market/design incentives and predictability when relying on cross-field analogies. This rationale aligns with KSR's discussion of variations across fields of endeavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation to modify/combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify explicit or implicit teachings, suggestions, or motivations in the prior art that would motivate modification or combination. Explain factual underpinning for the motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s reply must distinctly and specifically point out errors (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A blanket assertion is insufficient; address each ground with specific distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective traverse of factual findings requires reasoned statement and documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported reliance on common knowledge is substantively inadequate. Documentary evidence (affidavits/declarations) or reasoned argument is necessary; otherwise the Office may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office consideration of rebuttal evidence including secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including evidence of secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence should be evaluated in view of the entire record; all rejections and their bases should be reviewed for continued viability. Office actions should clearly articulate findings and how conclusions are supported by the findings. See MPEP § 2145 and §§ 716–716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal: inability to combine elements by known methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific factual evidence (experiments, declarations) showing technological barriers or incompatibilities that would have prevented combination by known methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal: combined elements do not merely perform separate functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue or show synergistic effects or interactions among elements that yield more than the sum of separate functions; provide supporting data or declarations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal: unexpected results from the claimed combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document unexpected results with comparative data, expert declarations, or other persuasive evidence showing results contrary to expectations from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available for use under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; admitted prior art can be relied upon regardless of statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 103 rejection is based on 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102 categories depending on the reference. For certain statutory-bar situations (e.g., pre-AIA 102(b) issues), see MPEP §§ 901, 2121–2129, 2151–2155 and MPEP § 2129 for admissions as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of prior art determined at time invention was made to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must ‘cast the mind back’ to the time the invention was made and avoid hindsight. See MPEP § 2145 subsection X.A and cases such as W.L. Gore v. Garlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to establish common ownership or joint research
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants the benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that the subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or that joint research conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish joint research provisions, applicant must show: (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP §§ 2146.01–.02 and Ex parte Yoshino.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must be analogous art to be relied upon under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). To support a determination of reasonable pertinence, the examiner may include a statement of understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art would have commended itself to an inventor. Consider the specification's reflection of the problem when assessing applicant arguments about nonanalogous art (Bigio, ICON Health, Klein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function when assessing analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: While classification and cross-references provide some evidence, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry far greater weight in determining whether art is analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh structural and functional overlap between the reference and claimed invention. Provide factual explanation of similarities/differences to justify reliance on the reference (see In re Ellis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts‑specific analogy considerations (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous art determinations should account for examples and practices in particular arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design), as precedent demonstrates field-specific considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedential examples: chemical arts where references concerned with absorbing biologically active materials were pertinent (Ex parte Bland); mechanical arts where similar device problems justify inter-field search (Stevenson, Bigio); electrical arts where solutions to rate-limiting problems are analogous (Medtronic); design arts per MPEP §1504.03 and cases such as Rosen, Pappas, Butera. Explain why the reference would be within the relevant field of endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the inventor's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention must be considered as a whole in difference analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on isolated differences; analyze the invention as a whole, including how disparate elements interact to produce an overall effect. Case examples (Stratoflex, Hirao) illustrate that admitted unobvious components can render the whole nonobvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill invention to a ‘gist’ or ‘thrust’ in place of whole analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narrowing the claim focus to a single advantage or feature that ignores express claim limitations; ensure the full claim scope and limitations are considered (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source of a problem can be part of the invention as a whole and may support patentability even if the remedy would have been obvious once the source was known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the discovery itself is supported by the specification or evidence; recognize that if prior art already contained the same solution for a similar problem, discovery may not render the invention patentable (In re Sponnoble, In re Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating the allegation, by affidavits/declarations or clear assertions in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient. Provide declarations or specification support to show the discovery and that it was not routine or known in the art (Kaslow, Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosed inherent properties are part of the 'as a whole' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In delineating the invention as a whole, look to properties of the subject matter which are inherent and disclosed in the specification; these inherent properties are considered in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inherent properties disclosed in the specification (e.g., chemical properties, performance parameters). However, obviousness cannot be predicated on features not known at the time the invention was made even if later shown to be inherent (In re Antonie, In re Rijckaert). See MPEP §2112 on inherency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety, including teachings that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be considered as a whole, including portions that would lead away from the claimed invention; teachings away can weigh against an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify portions of the reference that discourage the claimed approach; however, mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not necessarily teach away (In re Fulton). Provide factual analysis of whether the reference criticizes or discourages the claimed solution (W.L. Gore, Allied Erecting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art must be determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must determine the level of ordinary skill in the art when analyzing obviousness (heading: Factors to consider in determining level of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although factors are listed in the following section (not in this chunk), this is a required element of obviousness analysis; consider education, experience, and industry practice for the relevant time frame and cite supporting rationale.
